html:
The Bororo, who call themselves Boe, are an Indigenous people of Mato Grosso in central western Brazil. Their language belongs to the wider Macro-Jê family. Once spread over a large area, they now live on several small reserves.

Their villages are laid out in a circle around a men's house, and the whole community is divided into two halves whose members must marry into the other. Their funerals are long and elaborate, lasting weeks or months.

The French anthropologist Claude Lévi-Strauss studied them in 1935 and wrote about them in "Tristes Tropiques", which made them famous. Brazilian telegraph lines across their land in the early 1900s were led by Cândido Rondon, himself of partly Bororo descent, and Salesian missions settled among them from 1902. Their neighbours to the south are the Terena.
